ruh0: Mood Check: WHO-5 Well-Being and PHQ-4 Anxiety and Depression Screen | İhsan Eren
ruh1: Check how your last two weeks have been with the World Health Organization’s well-being index (WHO-5) and the PHQ-4 anxiety and depression screen: 9 questions, 2 minutes. What the scores mean, when to seek support, and tracking your results on your own device.
ruh3: Look back over the last two weeks with two short, widely used questionnaires: the World Health Organization’s well-being index (WHO-5) and the PHQ-4, which screens for symptoms of anxiety and depression. Nine questions in all, about two minutes. The results do not diagnose anything; they help you see when it may be time to seek support.

ruh73: The WHO-5 questions and answer options are taken from the official English version of the questionnaire. The developers of the PHQ-4 do not require permission to reproduce or translate it; the questions are shown in their original English wording.
ruh75: A five-question measure of well-being over the last two weeks, developed at the World Health Organization’s collaborating centre in mental health. It has been translated into more than 30 languages; according to a review of 213 studies, it is suitable both for depression screening and for monitoring treatment.
ruh76: The Turkish version was tested with 1,752 adults and older adults in primary care and showed high reliability.
ruh78: A very short screening questionnaire with two questions on anxiety and two on depression. It was developed with 2,149 patients in 15 primary care clinics in the United States. Higher scores went hand in hand with poorer daily functioning, more disability days and more use of health care.

ruh98: What the result does and does not tell you
ruh99: These questionnaires do not diagnose; they show whether a more detailed assessment may be needed. A diagnosis is made in a consultation with a doctor or a mental health professional.
ruh100: The result reflects only the last two weeks.
ruh101: Grief, severe stress, lack of sleep or a physical illness can affect the scores.
ruh102: A high symptom score does not mean there is definitely a problem; nor does a low score guarantee that all is well.
ruh103: If you feel unwell, talk to a professional whatever your score.

ruh113: My score was low; do I have depression?
ruh114: These questionnaires do not diagnose; they are screening tools that show whether a more detailed assessment is needed. A diagnosis is made in a consultation with a doctor or a mental health professional. If your score is below the cut-off, or you don’t feel well, talk to a professional.
ruh115: How often should I repeat it?
ruh116: Because the questions cover the last two weeks, repeating it every two weeks is enough. In research, a 10-point change in the well-being score is regarded as meaningful.
ruh117: My score is fine but I feel bad; what should I do?
ruh118: Short questionnaires cannot pick up everything. If you feel unwell, or your symptoms are affecting your daily life, see a doctor or a mental health professional whatever your score.
ruh119: If you are worried about someone close to you, talk to them and help them get support.
